    省委常委换届时的年龄线，在这轮换届已经顺延。 按往年的规矩，满58岁的省委常委*，全部应该到龄退休。2021年/2022年换届，所有的省委常委都符合了这个规矩，无一例外。最年长的留任者在换届时是57岁11个月。 这轮换届，已经有四个省委常委满58岁却继续留任。其中包含了一个省委副书记和一个常务副省长。你问我为什么省长越来越老，这就是原因——能够升任省长的梯队越来越老，这些老人不退休，占着位置，导致年轻人上不来。 * 不包括省委书记、省长、正部级省委副书记、省纪委书记、省军区领导media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    @cnpoliwatch2026年省级两会的人事调整，省委常委、副省长退居二线的年龄发生了变化。 按以前的标准，应该是以1966年6月/7月的出生年月划线。 今年的省级两会，却以1966年2月/3月划线： 出生于1966年2月及之前，补选为省人大常委会副主任或省政协副主席，退居二线。 出生于1966年3月及之后，继续担任一线职务。

    same dynamic played out with Agencies in the US before the global financial crisis. Treasury issuance lagged the growth in dollar fx reserves in a big way, forcing a range of investors to in effect treat Agencies as a safe assets .... 1/2post ↗原帖 ↗
    @ShortCircuit_KJAdam Tooze makes a useful point about bond markets that often gets inverted. When Germany barely issued new debt (debt brake + surpluses), Bunds became scarce. Bond traders and portfolio managers still need high-quality paper to buy, sell, and hold. So French OATs stepped in as the closest substitute. Demand for French bonds rose, prices went up, yields fell — and France temporarily joined the “high-quality” club alongside Germany. Scarcity of the safest asset doesn’t mean managers love thin markets. It means capital gets pushed into the next-best alternative until that scarcity eases. Once German issuance picked up and perceptions shifted, France’s spreads widened again.
    That obviously didn't work out -- but it was a very real dynamic. In mid 08 China held as many Agencies as Treasuries. And now of course the dynamic has been reversed -- US treasury issuance far exceeds organic demand for safe US dollar assets h/t to @NewLeftEViews for the link/ Tooze video 2/2post ↗原帖 ↗

    @YashengHuangIt also gets the Apple story wrong. The right version of that history is that Apple—and Foxconn—tapped into existing manufacturing capabilities in China. Before Apple, China already had a massive network of component producers and an incredibly skilled labor force. Apple repurposed and added some of these capabilities to iPhone production on top of that baseline. Apple should get the credit for jump starting handset production in China, but the spillover story is in the other direction as well. Apple went to China because of China’s existing general manufacturing capabilities in the first place and it was able to retool and upgrade these existing capabilities for its own production. That is not Arizona story at all.

    Imagine, for a second, if economic development and quality of life for Uyghurs in China/Xinjiang were substantially higher than the average citizen in Turkey itself. To continue this sport-competition analogy, that is a key "scorecard" that ultimately resolves online spats between fans of each side (although inevitably they will always find other things to squabble about). Some reality and relevant economic facts today related to that economic scorecard: 1⃣ Uyghurs in Xinjiang are arguably less economically developed than Turks in Turkey, at least as measured by nominal per capita GDP today: - Turkey is at ~$19k per capita GDP. Key caveat here that this nominal figure is highly sensitive to the Lira exchange rate, a real concern as Turkey's fiscal situation is precarious with most of its public and private debt denominated in foreign currencies. Turkey is also a major energy importer, more reliant on energy imports than even China on a % basis. As recently as 2018-22 during the last FX/economic crisis, nominal GDP was in the $9-11k range. - Xinjiang's per capita GDP will be ~$13k per capita in 2026 at prevailing exchange rates. However, this masks large socioeconomic divide between the largely urban Han population in the north and the rural-leaning Uyghur in the south. Based on urban/rural splits in disposable income, Uyghurs in Xinjiang are more in the ~$7-8k range. 2⃣ The gap has also closed meaningfully over the past four decades. Trajectory favors China in this case. In the 1980s, the ratio between Turkey's per capita GDP was ~8:1. In the 1990s it was ~6:1. In the 2000s, ~3:1. Today it is ~1.4:1 — again with the caveat that Uyghurs in Xinjiang are likely only ~3/5ths of the provincial average.post ↗原帖 ↗

    On China's new draft AI export controls, we have additional clarification from Yuyuantantian. The piece is trying to push back against any notion that China will impose sweeping export controls on AI. It emphasizes that it's business as usual for most AI models and services, like API services. It's just a few areas where Beijing wants control: sensitive national data, critical applications like defense, and key physical compute technologies. And there are some areas where Beijing wants more visibility, namely powerful AI models. The piece talks a lot about the importance of open-source AI and how AI governance and safety should not be controlled by a few frontier AI players but shaped and refined by different players around the world. DeepSeek and MiniMax have already completed registration and licensing for their open-source models. Overall, what's interesting to me is how much Beijing is trying to signal openness in the face of these export control measures. They don't to hurt China's AI industry overseas or international AI cooperation efforts. China is trying to find the delicate balance between adding more controls on what they see as a strategically important technology and supporting their global AI growth efforts.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    ARTEX, an open-source Chinese AI cyber tool, seems to be involved in a number of AI cyberattacks: Korean banks, Japanese firms, and now a Microsoft alert. Crucially, this is not an AI model. It’s a harness that can use any AI model—American or Chinese—to autonomously find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities in a given target. The original tool, developed by Chinese cybersecurity firm ThreatBook, was available as a public repo on GitHub that has since been removed. But forked versions seem to still exist on GitHub and elsewhere. Most interestingly, China’s new AI export controls seem to target tools like ARTEX, i.e. “AI-assisted vulnerability discovery technologies” 人工智能辅助漏洞挖掘技术. I wonder if this part of the export controls was added at the last minute to block a tool like ARTEX from being available outside China.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    American cancer patients are getting life-saving drugs from China that are not yet available in the US.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @maxdoppeltIn January 2025 my mom’s lung cancer spread to her brain. The drug with the best chance of helping her was approved in China but not here. A doctor told me, almost as an aside, that if she were Chinese she could buy it at a pharmacy. So I flew to Shanghai and came home with 26 boxes in my luggage. That was 19 months ago. My mom is still here, still working, and in her words has had an amazing three years. The drug was approved in China in 2023. The FDA approved it in July 2025. It still is not for sale here. I know of at least 30 Americans who have made the same trip. I have been scared to tell this story because I worried it could cost my mom access to the medicine keeping her alive. But the problem matters more than my silence. These drugs need to be developed and available here, and that means FDA reform. Art Allen at KFF Health News told our story this week. It also ran in The Washington Post. https://kffhealthnews.org/health-industry/china-cancer-drugs-foreign-travel-pharma-biotech-fda-regulation-clinical-trials/

I would say it’s even possibly a racist thing to believe that we can be so much better than China and the Chinese people that we’ll just beat them with a tiny fraction of the population. We need to do better with what we’ve got. But we also just need a lot more people. We need 1 billion Americans minimum, probably more like 2 or 3 billion, with better demographics and better natural resources. The Dutch once had the most powerful navy in the world. They didn’t lose that position because they fell behind on factories or shipbuilding. They became economically irrelevant.” Both countries are competing with respect to declining birth rates. Both nations must be more willing to have children and expand the population growth exponentially over the next decade. The current economic path is unsustainable if our labor force begins to shrink even with artificial intelligence on the rise.

    @kyleichanTo clarify, I still think Chinese FDI can offer tech benefits to the US through two channels: 1. Older tech: China's export controls put limits on transferring cutting-edge tech. But ironically I see this as enabling greater transfer of older generation tech. Beijing is encouraging Chinese companies to invest overseas while setting some boundaries on what can be shared rather than leaving this up to private firms. 2. Informal know-how: Arguably much if not most of China's gains from foreign tech were not in formal IP transfer, which foreign firms guarded closely, but from informal know-how. When you build a new plant and train a bunch of local staff and work with local suppliers, this can have huge positive spillovers far beyond engineering blueprints and design patents. For example, a lot of China's edge in LFP batteries is knowing how to reliably and efficiently scale production. China will not make tech transfer easy. But neither did the US or other countries when they invested in China. Ultimately it boils down to how hard the host country bargains and what forms of leverage they can bring to bear. And the US has tremendous leverage, particularly at a time when Chinese firms are desperate for overseas markets. Re-upping my piece on how China did this with FDI: https://www.highcapacity.org/p/chinas-faustian-bargain

    To clarify, I still think Chinese FDI can offer tech benefits to the US through two channels: 1. Older tech: China's export controls put limits on transferring cutting-edge tech. But ironically I see this as enabling greater transfer of older generation tech. Beijing is encouraging Chinese companies to invest overseas while setting some boundaries on what can be shared rather than leaving this up to private firms. 2. Informal know-how: Arguably much if not most of China's gains from foreign tech were not in formal IP transfer, which foreign firms guarded closely, but from informal know-how. When you build a new plant and train a bunch of local staff and work with local suppliers, this can have huge positive spillovers far beyond engineering blueprints and design patents. For example, a lot of China's edge in LFP batteries is knowing how to reliably and efficiently scale production. China will not make tech transfer easy. But neither did the US or other countries when they invested in China. Ultimately it boils down to how hard the host country bargains and what forms of leverage they can bring to bear. And the US has tremendous leverage, particularly at a time when Chinese firms are desperate for overseas markets.     @cnpoliwatch新一轮省级党委换届，已经拉开帷幕。 上一轮省级党委换届，共产生了392人次*的省委常委，其中“70后”共有68人，占所有省级党委常委的17.3%，平均每省有2.2个“70后”省委常委。 68名“70后”省委常委，包括2名“70后”省委副书记（诸葛宇杰、时光辉）和4名“75后”省委常委（任维、张红文、张晓强、伊力扎提·艾合买提江）。 换届后，全国最年轻的省级党委常委是西藏党委常委、常务副主席任维（1976.05）。 这轮换届，“75后”省委常委还能有68个吗？还能有任何“75后”省委副书记吗？还能有任何“80后”省委常委吗？ * 对应388人；孟凡利、王成、张鸿星、徐海荣等四人在两省重复当选。
    解读中共省级党委换届 财新记者 陈宝成 2012年7月5日 2012年7月3日，新一届北京市委常委班子产生。至此，在2011年10月至11月、2012年4月至7月两个时间段，中共分阶段在31个省份完成省级党委换届。这意味着中共十八大之前的省级党委常委布局告一段落。 本轮省级党委换届共产生常委404人（次），新疆、西藏各15人，青海14人，辽宁等24省份各13人，海南、陕西、四川、上海各12人；其中王三运在安徽、甘肃，尹德明在西藏、天津均曾分别当选常委。 各省份党委换届后，中央曾调整了河南、安徽、江西、内蒙古、西藏、湖南个别常委。截至目前，河南、内蒙古常委各缺额一名，现任省级党委常委实有402人。 “革命化、年轻化、知识化、专业化”是新时期中共干部政策的指导方针，选拔任用干部坚持德才兼备，以德为先，讲究来自“五湖四海”，注重选拔女性干部，并重视发挥共青团的“后备军”作用。本轮省级党委换届结果体现了上述因素。 与五年前的上一轮省级党委换届相比，现任省级党委常委的年龄段分布呈现“40后”逐步淡出、“50后”已成主导、“60后”异军突起的特点。 财新记者统计，现任省级党委常委仅有“40后”8人，占1.99%；“50后”277人，占68.91%，从而在中国省级政要中占据绝对优势；“60后”117人，占29.10%。 其中最年长的是出生于1945年4月的上海市委书记俞正声，最年轻的是出生于1968年7月的福州市委书记杨岳，前者是17届中央政治局委员。 从上一轮换届后，“60后”省级党委常委数量剧增，从34人增长到117人，增幅达三倍多；分布的省份也从原来的24个扩展到目前的所有省份。 现任“60后”省级党委常委最多的是新疆、西藏和贵州，各有七人；其次是内蒙古、安徽、黑龙江，各有六人；山西、吉林、宁夏各有五人，位居第三。 从我国地区分布看，东、中、西部“60后”省级党委常委的数量分别是35、32、50，明显体现出向中西部地区倾斜的特点。 有六位“60后”担任省级党政一把手。他们分别是内蒙古的胡春华、吉林的孙政才、湖南的周强，以及新疆的努尔•白克力、福建的苏树林、河北的张庆伟。在省级党委专职副书记中，“60后”达8人之多；其中河北、福建两省的所有省委副书记均是“60后”。 不过与上一轮换届相比，本次省级党委换届“干部年轻化”的说法值得商榷。据财新记者统计，仅有安徽、内蒙古、河北三省份常委的平均年龄有所降低，其余28省份常委平均年龄均有所升高；其中辽宁平均年龄最大，河北和新疆平均年龄最小。 “知识化”和“专业化”集中体现在“博士常委”群体的涌现。 财新记者统计，“博士常委”有100位，占现任省级党委常委总数的24.88%。这意味着几乎每四位省级党委常委中就有一位“博士常委”。 其中，天津有七位排名居首，其次是山西有六位，而河北、陕西、甘肃则分别以五位“博士常委”排名第三。若按照地区分布，东、中、西部分别有“博士常委”32、30、38人，分布较为均衡。 百位“博士常委”所学专业学科呈多元化分布趋势。财新记者统计，共有经济学博士32位，管理学博士27位，法学博士15位，工学博士13位，哲学博士和农学博士各三位，教育学博士、历史学博士和文学博士各两位，理学博士和荣誉博士各一位；其中山西省纪委书记李兆前是唯一的工学和管理学“双博士”。 此外，六位省级党委常委曾在任领导职务时有博士后研究经历，分别是：山西的袁纯清、江西的姚亚平、贵州的李军、重庆的翁杰明、河北的赵勇和聂辰席。 百位“博士常委”中包括十名正省级高官，分别是辽宁、山西、广西、吉林4省（区）委书记和云南、安徽、浙江、宁夏、青海、天津六省份行政一把手；其余90位为副省级高官。 “博士常委”的性别比呈现“阳盛阴衰”的特点：有男性92人，女性8人；从年龄段看，“50后”62人，远远多于“60后”的38人。 少数“博士常委”在从政前完成了博士学习。如新疆的熊选国师从刑法学权威马克昌，博士毕业后入最高法院并升至副院长。 与之类似的还有辽宁的王珉、江西的尚勇、广东的王荣、湖南的陈肇雄、辽宁的夏德仁、山西的李兆前、福建的杨岳、新疆的黄卫、海南的李秀领、吉林的孙政才、江西的姚亚平等。 但更多“博士常委”在任领导职务时获博士头衔。财新记者统计，百位“博士常委”中有78人在任政学商界职务时获博士学位，有10人读博时不任任何领导职务，另有12人读博时任职情况不详。 如青海的骆惠宁在任安徽省委常委、宣传部长和青海省委副书记期间，先后获得中国科技大学管理学硕士和中国人民大学经济学博士，用时仅三年七个月。 获博士学位较快的是河北的梁滨和江西的史文清。前者获中国社科院研究生院博士学位耗时一年九个月；后者获西安交通大学产业经济学专业博士历时两年三个月。 甘肃的虞海燕攻读东北大学材料所材料学专业博士研究生，历时八年四个月；江苏的李小敏从2002年9月起攻读南京大学城市发展战略专业在职博士研究生，至今已九年多。 博士头衔的获得与官员短时间内的升迁有统计学上的正相关。财新记者统计，在完成读博的一年内，袁纯清等33人被安排到更加重要的岗位，李秀领、姚亚平则很快告别学院而走上仕途，占百名“博士常委”的35%。 在获得博士学位后继续从事学术的人中，王珉六年后任南京航空学院副校长，又四年多后任江苏省省长助理，从而踏上政坛；尚勇、陈肇雄、夏德仁、李兆前、黄卫、孙政才、王荣、柯尊平、朱丽萍等人也走过了大同小异的“学而优则仕”之路。 在本省或临近省份攻读博士，成为不少“博士常委”的选择。如吉林的马俊清、金振吉、高广滨和曾任吉林省委常委的李斌，都在吉林大学攻读博士学位；河北的聂辰席、景春华、田向利博士学位均来自天津大学。 本轮省级党委换届结束后，共有37位“巾帼常委”，占现任省级党委常委的9.20%。其中江苏女常委有三人之多，其次是安徽、辽宁、福建、贵州、甘肃各有两人，山东等24省份各有一人。由于原党委常委崔玉英调离，西藏成为目前唯一没有“巾帼常委”的省份。 37位“巾帼常委”中，福建的孙春兰是省委书记，安徽的李斌是省长，两人也分别是现任唯一的女性省级党政一把手；上海的殷一璀已任三届市委副书记，重庆的张轩则是首次连任市委副书记。 在其他担任省级党委常委的女性中，江西的舒晓琴是唯一的女性省委政法委书记兼公安厅长；天津的朱丽萍是市教育工委书记；还有两位是省委秘书长，两位是地级市市委书记，三位为省委组织部长，三位是省级工会主席，五位是纪委书记，五位是宣传部长，六位是统战部长，七位是省级政府副职。 其中，贵州省常务副省长谌贻琴兼任省委宣传部长，海南省纪委书记马永霞兼任省检察院检察长，湖北省副省长张岱梨兼任省委统战部长。 402名省级党委常委来自全国31个省份，体现出干部任用的“五湖四海”原则；与此同时，干部储备的地区差别呈明显的阶梯状分布。 从省委常委们的籍贯分布看，走出10位以上省委常委的有14个省份，分别是山东、河北、江苏、浙江、河南、湖北、辽宁、安徽、湖南、陕西、山西、四川、福建和云南。其中前七省籍省委常委即达204人，超过全部常委的一半。 22个省份中有来自山东籍的常委53人。这一数字比排名最后十位的北京、天津、宁夏、青海、内蒙古、新疆、上海、海南、甘肃、西藏籍常委总和还要多7人。排名次席的是河北，有30人分布于16省份；第三位是江苏，有29人分布于19省份。 本省籍常委在各自省份常委班子中占多数的，有北京、重庆、江苏、安徽、河北、山东、河南、陕西、宁夏、山西、辽宁、吉林、浙江、江西、湖北、湖南、四川、内蒙古、新疆、福建、广东、广西、云南等23省份；其中山东以9人、山西以7人占据绝对多数。 据财新记者统计，来自东、中、西部地区的省级党委常委分别有195、122、85人。这说明干部储备培养的地区差别与中国经济社会发展的地区差别大致暗合。 在402位省级党委常委中，有168人曾有各级共青团工作经历，占41.79%。其中七人担任所在省份党政一把手。他们是安徽省委书记张宝顺、黑龙江省委书记吉炳轩、山西省委书记袁纯清、四川省委书记刘奇葆、湖南省委书记周强、内蒙古单位书记胡春华和山东省长姜大明。 在各省份有共青团系统任职经历的省委常委中，贵州九人最多，其次是广东和天津各有八人，排在第三位的是山东和陕西各有七人。按照地区分布，东、中、西部分别有63、44、61位省级党委常委曾任职于各级共青团系统，分布较为均衡。 其中，曾任团中央书记处书记以上职务者有14人，而且其年龄分布较为平均，有“50后”6人，“60后”8人。 按照以往惯例，中共全国代表大会后，会有一些省份党政高官调整职务。这意味着目前的省级党委领导班子，仍有可能会在十八大之后进行一定规模的调整。post ↗原帖 ↗

    NYT: "Surging exports and the industrial production needed to sustain them kept China’s economy growing over the past three months, even as consumer spending stagnated and investment plunged. The result is an economy increasingly dependent on selling goods abroad, even as domestic demand deteriorates." NYT's Keith Bradsher gets this right. Many other analysts have been presenting this year's economic data as describing a two-track economy, with a sluggish domestic economy being balanced by a brilliant export economy. But that is a very poor description of what is actually happening. Yes, net exports are surging, but this isn't a sign of a viable export sector. If the export sector were very profitable, it might make sense to describe it this way, but exports aren't especially profitable except in relation to domestic sales, where except in a few sectors businesses are struggling to make any profit at all, and once direct and indirect subsidies are backed out, much of China's exports are net value destroyers for the economy, with the losses capitalized on balance sheets in the form of surging debt. When an economy produces far more than it can absorb through domestic consumption or investment, it must either export the balance or close down domestic production. Given how high real unemployment is, especially among the young, Beijing has no choice but to force the former, even if this comes at an economic cost. The surge in China's net exports, in other words, is not a sigh of a strong and profitable export sector. If it takes rising debt, continued subsidies, and growing exports in order to prevent a contraction in domestic production, the surge in net exports is simply another way of describing weak domestic demand. Surging exports are usually a good sign for an economy. Surging net exports usually are not. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/business/china-economy-gdp.html?smid=tw-sharepost ↗原帖 ↗

  • 11:40 · @michaelxpettis Michael Pettis
    None of the data that came out today gives us a different picture of the Chinese economy from what we’ve seen all year. The economy is still heavily focused on boosting production and is still struggling with boosting demand. GDP grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, slightly higher than expected, from 5.0% in the first quarter and 4.3% in the second quarter. Year to date GDP has grown 4.6%, just above the bottom of the GDP growth target for 2026. In September, industrial output went up by 5.5% year on year, or 5.3% for the first nine months. Meanwhile retail sales increased by 1.1% in September, or 2.6% for the first nine months. The gap between domestic production and domestic consumption, in other words, continues to widen rather than narrow, with the gap much wider in September than it has been over the rest of the year. This can only be balanced by rising investment or a rising trade surplus. And it clearly isn’t being balanced by rising investment. Fixed asset investment in the first nine months of 2026 was down 7.2% year on year, or 4.2% with property investment deducted. The decline in overall investment was driven by an even sharper decline in private investment, which was down by 10.4% year on year, or 6.7% with property investment deducted. Disaggregated by sector, investment in infrastructure declined by 4.2% year on year, manufacturing by 2.1%, and real estate development by 20.6%. The good news is that the decline in investment may finally be bottoming out, with fixed asset investment in September, rising by 0.07% month on month. We will probably see fiscal expansion in the last quarter of this year, although I think it would be a good thing if Beijing let growth come in at the bottom of the target, especially if they lower the target further in 2027. Debt is simply growing too fast, and it is growing fast only because of the urgent desire to meet politically-determined GDP growth targets. The longer this goes on, the more difficult the ultimate adjustment will be. https://english.news.cn/20261019/2da9b2afcdaf42d3a3f009c338edd92a/c.htmlpost ↗原帖 ↗

    @jukan05This is a really interesting chart. I attended the TrendForce San Francisco roadshow yesterday, and this chart got me thinking about a lot of things. China is now expected to localize more than half, or close to half, of most equipment categories, excluding lithography and track. What does this mean? It means China can now expand mature node capacity far more easily than before, using equipment made domestically within China. Mature node foundries are booming right now, right? That's thanks to the AI supercycle driving demand for PMICs, power semiconductors, and so on. Samsung and TSMC shutting down their mature node capacity has also helped a lot. But here's what I imagine... that China could oversupply mature foundry capacity. Think about it. If China can be self sufficient in equipment, there's no limit to how far it can expand capacity. Then are companies like TI, with large revenue exposure to China, really safe? I think it's time to take another look at Western mature foundry companies with a high share of China revenue. Of course, I'm not saying sell TI right now. I'm just saying we should think about whether it makes sense to hold them for 10 years or more, like Coca Cola. If you have a different view, please feel free to share it. I’d love to learn.

  • 23:26 · @GlennLuk Glenn Luk
    The People have already voted with their feet/wallets: Out of an annual ~220M direct journeys b/n Beijing & Shanghai, >90% of them are via HSR. Today, ~half of air travel b/n Beijing & Shanghai is part of a multi-leg journey (e.g. transfer in Beijing to an international flight). HSR frees up airport capacity for routes that the rail network does not serve well. For directly connected major city pairs <1,500 km like Beijing-Shanghai, HSR is (i) faster door-to-door, (ii) more comfortable, (iii) more reliable and (iv) less expensive by 20-60% when comparing realized ticket prices (2nd class HSR vs. economy air).post ↗原帖 ↗
    @TGTM_Official“China vs US is no contest. Beijing–Nanjing 1,018 km, HSR 3 h 14 min at 350 km/h. SF–LA is shorter yet takes 5–6 hours by car. California HSR only reaches Merced–Bakersfield by 2032, full SF–LA maybe 2050.” Classic selective framing. They compare pure HSR station-to-station time with US door-to-door car (or implied flight hassle). Do the same for China and the picture changes: • Beijing–Nanjing HSR second class is typically 443–550 yuan for 3.5–4.5 hours point-to-point. • Discounted flights on the same route frequently go for 210–400 yuan (with fees often ~280–500). Air time is ~1.75–2 hours. Chinese travel sites repeatedly note that mid-week or off-peak flights undercut HSR, sometimes by a large margin. A round-trip flight can cost less than one-way HSR. • Door-to-door for a Chinese flight still includes airport transfers (often 1+ hour each side), security, and boarding—but often than not, these posters doesn’t really talk about the hassle of riding HSR as they have to go through the same security checks comparable China’s HSR network is large and fast on core corridors. It is also debt-heavy (railway group liabilities in the trillions of yuan), with most lines unprofitable and some stations underused. Treating point-to-point HSR speed as proof of overall superiority while ignoring cost, utilization, and the existence of cheaper flights on the exact same route is the propaganda pattern, not a rigorous comparison.

    My initial reaction to China's new AI export controls: They're confusing because they seem to be creating restrictions for China AI exports while simultaneously signaling continued "automatic" approval for open-source models. I don't think it's about leverage. I think China is generally worried about cyberattack potential for Chinese AI systems and don't want these proliferating outside China and then potentially hitting Chinese critical infrastructure or government systems. So the toughest restrictions--the prohibitions 禁止出口--are on AI autonomous malicious code generation. But there are also broad restrictions 限制出口 on AI models of above certain performance thresholds. Ministry of Commerce later said open-source models would be "automatically" approved upon registration, but then it does lay the groundwork for a more systematic monitoring of models and possible real restrictions later on. The part that's confusing to me is that AI systems that can help produce malware basically include all the top Chinese open-source models. And yet they're simultaneously "automatically" approved? It seems like this set of new export controls were created by one part of the bureaucracy that's worried about proliferation of harmful AI capabilities but then another part is trying to say "but actually we still support open-source." This is at least my initial reaction--my views may change as I re-read and re-analyze.post ↗原帖 ↗

  • 06:30 · @kevinsxu Kevin Xu
    I have been tracking US data center moratoriums since January. Built a public dashboard on my fund's website in March that has now been cited and linked in more places I can remember I have been mostly tracking, observing, thinking, and analyzing as this issue becomes front and center (and controversial) Now that the total count has crossed 400, here is my opinion on the whole thing as a responsible, AI bull. I have built an investment fund focused on AI. I want AI to go well. I'm incentivized for AI to go well. And I think these moratoriums are actually good for AI's long-term success and will help it go well, in all sorts of ways. Here's why: - these moratoriums squeeze out bad actors. Shady, disreputable so-called data center operators, who simply want to make a quick buck amidst the boom. There are many in the industry right now, as compute capacity continues to be limited. They don't engage with local communities, they hide behind NDAs or opaque corporate structures, and they likely won't build anything. Will sign some leases, take out some loans, and run. These moratoriums puts a lid on these bad actors, and force the good actors who might've wanted to cut corners for speed to dothe right things for the long-haul. - ironically, a slower pace of construction caused by these moratoriums keeps supply of compute even tighter, raises GPU rental prices, extends their usefulness. This is an inadvertently good outcome for AI broadly, as the ROI question is still up in the air, while the debt question is becoming front and center. A healthy GPU price will keep the current data center operators, mostly good ones who can build and want to build for the long-run, in a solid financial state, as AI adoption in enterprises and consumers settles into a predictable trajectory. Adoption always take longer than technologists think they should, but shorter than the Average Joe can adapt. Most people don't live and breathe this stuff, nor should they. - relatedly, these moratoriums will increase the likelihood of a "slower for longer" trajectory per @GavinSBaker. It's almost like a "soft landing" in Fed speak. Why do I think so? If you look at all these 400+ moratoriums (meaning pauses, not bans), the vast majority of them are one year long or shorter, stretching into mid to late 2027. Communities don't not want data centers, but they don't want them shoved down their throat. They need time to learn about them, in the same way that companies and consumers want time to learn about the latest, greatest AI agents. The industry has about a year or so to do meaningful education and engagement (not just PR and ads, those don't work). Meanwhile the data centers already in motion will keep most of the supply chain humming for two years without noticing any interruptions, per $CIEN CEO Gary Smith (listen to his last earnings call). - What should the industry address for communities Air noise pollution is real. Most of these data center locations are in rural areas, which is quiet, beautiful and tolerance for industrial noise is low. Water is a tricky one because, yes, liquid cooling is closed loop, but most existing data centers are either air cooled or situated next to large rivers to provide water based cooling. Communities have their priors when it comes to water's role. This requires not ads or tech bro sermons, but real product demos of new liquid cooling solutions in city council meetings. Don't lecture, show and educate. - Lastly, keep in mind that this wave of moratoriums is bipartisan, not a liberal anti-tech pet issue. Nothing in history has united more avowed socialists and die-hard MAGAs than data centers. Throwing China out there as the foreign boogeyman won't work. I have talked to several people, some sitting city council members, some activists, all of whom are aware of the China angle, misinformation or competition, none of them are convinced by it. Treat local issues seriously and literally, not toss out boogeyman to distract, will go a long way for AI and tech to go well.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    @DavidSacksAre Small Models Really a Threat? The Anthropic Fear Factory just released a new report warning that small models may be only months away from self-replicating across cheap IoT devices like off-brand Android TV boxes and smart ovens. They say such an AI worm would be hard to shut down since there’s no central kill switch. We’ve gone from “The Terminator is coming” to “your toaster might kill you.” But the experiments don’t support the dramatic headlines. They ran a 26B model across 15 $55 TV boxes at 0.39 tokens per second. The end-to-end test used emulated devices with deliberately open ADB ports, so the “hacking” step was trivial. The capable model often ran on a separate server. Agents were harnessed and told to propagate. This is not proof of autonomous rogue AI worms in the wild. Nor is the threat even novel. Worms that do this without AI already exist. Mirai in 2016 scanned for default credentials and built massive DDoS botnets. Kimwolf has infected over two million devices, mostly cheap Android TV boxes, by hitting open ADB ports. Small models don’t currently add much that matters on these targets. The bottleneck has never been figuring out the device. It’s the huge number of devices that ship with open ports, default passwords, and no patching. Traditional worms already exploit that at scale. A practical attacker would use the best models available offline to design a better traditional worm, then ship the lean binary. You get the intelligence benefit at design time without dragging a slow, heavy model along with every infection. Embedding a weak model in the payload is the worse option for anyone who actually wants the largest, fastest botnet. The timing of Anthropic’s latest scare campaign is hard to ignore. The day before, Brian Armstrong posted that Coinbase fine-tuned an open-weight small model (Qwen-3.5-9B) on proprietary fraud data. It beat frontier models, including Anthropic’s own Opus 4.5, while being faster and much cheaper. In testing it cut fraudulent transactions by about 30%. This is the emerging pattern. For narrow enterprise workloads you don’t need a general superintelligence. You need a small specialist model trained on your own data. Cheaper to run, especially as compute gets tighter, and often better on the metric that matters. That is a direct threat to the frontier-company model of selling access to ever-larger general models. Safety advocates should be welcoming this development. If the real concern is existential risk from ever-larger frontier systems — the ones that could theoretically do sustained autonomous R&D or become hard to control — then a shift toward smaller specialized models is the safer outcome. Small models specialized on fraud detection or support tickets are not pushing the frontier. They are not in the category of systems that could become a new species. The theoretical loss-of-control risk is created by models getting bigger and more generally capable. Safety advocates focused on those risks should welcome companies having a cheaper alternative to constantly scaling general models. Instead we get dramatic warnings about small models at the exact moment they are starting to take real enterprise share from closed-model companies like Anthropic.

    @RnaudBertrandThis has got to be the most moronic story of the month. It's genuinely so stupid it frankly boggles the mind. It was broken by Norwegian daily "Dagens Næringsliv" (DN) under the title "Chinese-owned rental cars filmed secret exercise: Saved video of soldiers and codes" (https://www.dn.no/forsvar-og-sikkerhet/kinesisk-eide-leiebiler-filmet-hemmelig-ovelse-lagret-video-av-soldater-og-koder/2-1-2050958). BUT when you look into the story what actually happened is that, for an exercise, the Norwegian army was short on cars so it rented some from Hertz. Those rental cars had dashcams - as cars do - that the soldiers mistakenly kept on. At one point, some soldiers found out about that: they were clicking through the car menus out of boredom and stumbled on the footage, including clips of themselves typing gate codes in front of the camera. They deleted the footage. There is zero evidence the footage left the car. THAT'S IT, that's the whole story. China hysteria being what it is in Europe these days, this somehow got transformed into a "China spying" story because Hertz Norway is owned by Volvo, itself owned by Geely (a Chinese company), and 2 of the cars were from a Chinese brand, Deepal. The narrative apparently being that Geely, through Volvo, through Hertz, deliberately left standard dashcams on in rental cars in the hope that the Norwegian military would one day rent them and forget to turn the dashcams off 🤦 And now, as is always the case, it's being spread globally by accounts like Clash Report 👇, which even found a way to make the story dumber: their version has the cars as "Chinese-owned Volvos", when they weren’t Volvos at all. Such is the contemporary media ecosystem: one outlet invents the hysteria, the next one strips away the last remaining nuance and we all end up dumber for it.

    @RnaudBertrandExtremely wise words by Shivshankar Menon, India's former Foreign Secretary and National Security Advisor. Asked by the host what worries him about India - what is a burden of history for India - he replied that "there is such a thing as excessive pride in your past." He explains that talking of "your glorious golden ages in the past" to "feel good about yourself" is ok - a normal aspect of building an identity for yourself - but "when you then carry it on into victimhood and into revenge for history" and when that becomes a driving force for today's actions, then it becomes "dangerous." He takes the example of people in India speaking about "a thousand years of slavery" (meaning Muslim and then British rule) or of Chiang Kai-shek writing every night in the top right of his diary "never forget national humiliation" (I checked and he actually wrote 雪耻 - xuě chǐ - which means "avenge the humiliation": https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_1680286, he did it from 1928 until his last diary entry in July 1972). It's a wise point in general: when you think about it, nationalism isn't necessarily destructive in and of itself. But it becomes so when you convince yourself as a nation or people that you are a victim and that there is a guilty party. Because, as Menon puts it, it makes you "stop dealing with reality as it is" and leads to "counterproductive policy and ideas." All the more dangerous because it’s so easy: nothing easier as a people, or as the ruler of a nation, than to blame others for what’s wrong. It spares you the much harder work of looking at your own failings, and absolves the rulers of responsibility. And the inverse is really hard: nothing harder when you have indeed been a victim than to resist turning that grievance into a political program, and to instead focus on what you can actually build today - which often involves working hand in hand with the guilty party. Which is, incidentally, why what China did was so impressive. It could have turned national humiliation into policies of revenge and hatred but instead chose to define it largely as China's own mistake for having been weak enough that foreigners could take advantage of that (Xi Jinping himself defines it that way in his book: https://x.com/RnaudBertrand/status/2069979487354405281). Which is constructive, because then the objective isn't revenge but building yourself, and China did that working hand in hand with the West. We’re seeing some version of victimhood drive policies in too many countries around the world. Europe is, sadly, a case in point: Russia and China have become the all-purpose explanation for almost every problem on the continent, from energy prices to deindustrialization. Very practical for EU leaders who never have to answer for their own choices... It's a good rule of thumb to have: if any politician builds his message around blame, take it as a red flag. That's what you reach for when you won't build. This is the source video, by the way: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IQ2ns6-CY-M On the WorldView Postcast of my friend @Hansong_Li

    @int_mon_econPerry Mehrling, RIP. According to the History of Economics Society, Perry Mehrling died "Monday night from injury sustained in a fall several days earlier." He was Professor of International Political Economy at Boston University and, previously, longtime Professor of Economics at Barnard College. He was a highly esteemed historian of economics. Here is his homepage: https://sites.bu.edu/perry/ His last book: "Money and Empire: Charles P. Kindleberger and the Dollar System" https://amzn.to/47RVhJ2 "Charles Kindleberger ranks as one of the twentieth century's best known and most influential international economists. This book traces the evolution of his thinking in the context of a 'key-currency' approach to the rise of the dollar system, here revealed as the indispensable framework for global economic development since World War II. Unlike most of his colleagues, Kindleberger was deeply interested in history, and his economics brimmed with real people and institutional details. His research at the New York Fed and BIS during the Great Depression, his wartime intelligence work, and his role in administering the Marshall Plan gave him deep insight into how the international financial system really operated. A biography of both the dollar and a man, this book is also the story of the development of ideas about how money works. It throws revealing light on the underlying economic forces and political obstacles shaping our globalized world." Charles Goodhart: "The discipline of economics is balanced, somewhat unsteadily, between two legs, with the skill of the historian on one side and of the mathematical modeler on the other. In the second half of the 20th century, the tide flowed strongly to elevate the second leg and to diminish the first. In this delightful biography of Charlie Kindleberger, a charming and loveable man, Perry Mehrling shows how Charlie, in his chosen role, as an international monetary economist, fought against that tide, often unsuccessfully. Perry writes so beautifully that one would only need a smattering of economics to enjoy the tale; while if one is interested in the history of economic thought in international monetary economics, then this book is, of course, a must read.' https://amzn.to/47RVhJ2

If this were being treated as commercial espionage, it would be supported by DOJ's Criminal Division. (3) Abdulrahman Alfozan has ties to Saudi Arabia, the Saudi government, and the Saudi royal family. In addition to being a Saudi national, he is a Venture Partner at RAED Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm whose investors include multiple Saudi government-owned funds. One of two other venture partners at RAED is Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family. (4) If Alfozan was acting in coordination with the Saudi government, I do not see how any company could possibly host a frontier AI model in Saudi Arabia after this incident. If Saudi intelligence services are spying on US frontier AI companies inside the United States, they surely are closely tracking everything these labs are doing in Saudi Arabia--and would almost certainly have access to any model weights hosted in Saudi Arabia. These weights are not only incredibly valuable IP, but increasingly provide national-asset-level defense and intelligence capabilities. US AI capabilities have to be protected from foreign espionage, which is exactly why DOJ charged Alfozan. (5) As a reminder, Saudi Arabia also maintains extensive and continuing ties to China in the AI space. It was recently reported that Saudi Arabia's AI national champion, Humain, is building its own AI model by using a Chinese open-source model from MiniMax as the base--and using US chips to train it. Huawei also maintains an extensive presence in Saudi Arabia. (6) If the Saudi government is indeed involved with this incident, and particularly given the longstanding concerns about Saudi Arabia's ties to China in the AI space and the rapidly increasing sensitivity of frontier AI technology, we have no choice but to immediately reexamine our AI relationship with Saudi Arabia. Last year Commerce approved licenses for 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell AI chips to Saudi Arabia. But if we can't trust Saudi Arabia not to steal any US models that it hosts, it makes zero sense to sell them any AI chips--especially given right now they're using these chips to fine-tune Chinese models. Stealing US AI models while building its ecosystem on top of Chinese models would be the exact opposite of supporting the US AI stack. If the Saudi government is involved, there must be consequences.

    This is a good piece overall but I do have a major quibble with the interpretation of this particular chart on "capital efficiency". 1⃣ The nature of capital investment in China vs. the U.S. is completely different (capital-light vs. capital-intensive) which makes direct country-to-country comparisons problematic. e.g. in my view the U.S. would be in a better strategic position today had it not shifted to such an extreme capital-light model (which helped it maintain those relatively high "productivity" levels): Our antiquated infrastructure and atrophied manufacturing ecosystem / supply chain were casualties of policies that shifted the economy to become "capital-light". Instead, I would argue the U.S. would be better off today if it had dedicated more resources investing in infrastructure, even if it lowered "capital efficiency" according to this metric. Said differently, high "capital efficiency" by this metric should not be interpreted as a universal positive, but also as a symptom of deeper structural issues. 2⃣ Meanwhile, I have argued how the downward trajectory on China's "capital efficiency ratio" was mainly a function of the shift from an export-processing intensive capital investment model in the 90s and 2000s to a housing and infrastructure-centric model since the mid/late-2000s and not declining capital efficiency. While RoIC in annualized % terms was lower on the latter, there is an offsetting effect with housing and infrastructure bearing significantly longer useful lives (meaning that you can spread economic payback over a longer period of time). Furthermore, infrastructure was comprised of significant "public goods" asset formation that generate significant externalities that are not necessarily captured in near/medium-term GDP.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    Capacity utilization in China’s automaker segment was 70.6% in the 1H of the year, down by ~1% YoY. China’s car manufacturing sector has been dragged down by foreign JVs for several years and this has only worsened in 2026. Unlike Chinese legacy ICE carmakers like Geely/Chery, foreign brands have not been able to meaningfully re-tool / re-direct ICE factory capacity for export markets or re-tool them for NEV production except in limited cases. Plummeting domestic ICE sales result in low (<50%) utilization rates at the JVs. If we exclude foreign brands, aggregate capacity utilization would be in the 78-83% range — which is considered healthy / normal. Leading pureplay NEV makers like BYD, Xiaomi, Tesla, Leapmotor and Aito are operating above this range (80-95%+) as are the EV segments for Chinese carmakers with legacy ICE operations like Geely and Chery. https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202607/t20260717_1964153.htmlmedia带图post ↗原帖 ↗
    Foreign JVs have not been able to meaningfully re-direct domestic factory ICE capacity. I have discussed key reasons for this in the past: 1) Their China factories were designed to serve only the Chinese domestic market. To serve markets outside China, they would need capex investment to re-tool … 2) Which would make little sense as they already have factories serving core markets that they do not want to cannibalize. 3) Their EV designs are typically not competitive enough to justify capital investment to re-tool for EV manufacturing. OTOH, Chinese incumbents like Geely, Chery and Chang’an have been able to re-direct domestic ICE capacity at foreign markets or re-tool them for NEV production to help keep ICE utilization rates relatively high.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @GlennLukWe also know that a disproportionate share of ICE under-utilization is with foreign JVs. Chinese ICE incumbent brands have been opening up new distribution overseas; exports have helped boost capacity utilization.

Given how energy intensive data centers are, electricity demand from AI data centers is on track to double globally within the next five years. Surging power demand from data centers is set to test the AI leaders’ power infrastructure, such as US, Europe and Japan, since their power capacities have barely grown in the past few decades. Assuming no acceleration in the construction of power generation, new data centers may absorb 48% of US’s incremental power supply between now and 2030. This may crowd out other sectors’ energy needs, pushing up energy prices. As such, these markets need to ramp up their investment in powering systems and grid infrastructure as data centers require stable and undisrupted power to ensure continuous operation. Consequently, this presents a huge opportunity for global power equipment manufacturers. Chinese producers are well positioned for this emerging industrial upturn as they ride on the tailwinds of higher export competitiveness especially after the pandemic.     @andrewbatsonThis is kind of a misleading framing, as the debt/GDP ratio is not going up because Xi is spending lavishly financed by debt; debt growth has slowed substantially and keeps slowing, but the ratio is still rising because nominal GDP growth has collapsed. Arguably in these conditions more debt-funded spending would not be "irresponsible" but responsible, because it could stabilize the nominal growth trajectory--at least that is the argument made by the many people who say more stimulus is needed.
    The Journal story suggested that rapid debt growth was somehow leading to export dependence (I guess b/c exports and debt are both going up) -- but I think that is a bit confused.     Chamath: The bottom line is that if you're picking a model/harness combo off a model-only leaderboard, you're making a critical decision based on only half the information.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @chamathModel Benchmarks Are Worthless How can a model score 24% and 59% on the same 113 coding tasks? It happens when you vary the harness that wraps it. I’ve increasingly ignored most of the recent model leaderboard results. Partly from exhaustion and partly because improvements in a ranking don’t show up in the actual work. So I asked the 8090 Labs team to measure what the leaderboards skip: the model and the harness together, on real bug fixes and features from open-source projects. 8090 Labs ran 7 models through 5 harnesses. Here are a few results I didn't expect: - Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 scored 41% in Claude Code and 61% in OpenAI's Codex. It made 28 tool calls at the median in one and 66 in the other. - The cheapest runs weren't the cheapest work. GLM in Codex cost $0.22 a run and $0.93 per success. In Pi it cost $0.25 a run and $0.43 per success. - GLM passed a task on both attempts 51 times in one harness and 16 times in another. - GPT-5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6 barely cared which harness they were in. The bottom line is that if you're picking a model/harness combo off a model-only leaderboard, you're making a critical decision based on only half the information. https://www.8090.ai/blog/same-model-different-harness?dub_id=5Ux9L6PBuBjhKzi7

    @karpathyDusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

    @BaldingsWorldThere is a clear asymmetry at play. The long term correlation is very low. What do I mean? Look at right side of the graph: the currency declined and exports grew above trend. That makes sense and it's observable. Now look at the left side: the currency grew significantly more expensive but exports kept growing on trend. This tells is two key things. First, there is a clear asymmetry in how Chinese trade responds to changes in the value of the RMB. Just because exports increase when the currency declined, do not expect exports to decline (or though not pictured here imports to increase). Second, there are clearly missing variables that would help explain why we are seeing the results we are seeing. As a simple example, the mass of Chinese over capacity is playing a significant role in boosting exports. This concept would be especially true considering imports. In short, do not expect a symmetric bounce in imports

  • 13:13 · @michaelxpettis Michael Pettis
    NYT: "Maros Sefcovic, the trade commissioner of the 27-nation bloc, said that the understanding could lead to China’s halving the number of hybrid gasoline-electric cars that it sends to the European Union in the next four years." This may seem like a victory, but the problem is a systemic one, and not sectoral. Because this agreement does not in any way address either China's demand imbalance or the overall role of the EU in absorbing that imbalance, it won't have much effect on overall EU manufacturing. All that will happen is a shift in the locus of net manufacturing imports from China, so that EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers. For historical reasons, trade discussions are usually held on a product-by-product basis, but while that may make sense in a world of broadly balanced trade, it makes no sense in a world of deep, persistent imbalances. China runs huge surpluses not because it produces too many hybrids but rather because of its deep consumption imbalance and the very low household income share of GDP. As long as that happens, the only recourse for the EU, if it does not want to accept deindustrialization, is either to reduce its own household share of GDP (which would be politically disruptive as well as bad for the global economy) or to intervene in its external accounts in such a way that it reverses the competitive impact of China's low household share of GDP. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/china-european-union-trade.html?smid=tw-sharepost ↗原帖 ↗

    @DavidSacksSatya is right. The way to make SI safe is not to train it with a sense of self, its own moral philosophy, and permission to act as a conscientious objector. That’s the “alignment” approach and it magnifies the control problem. The engineering approach that Satya describes is different: separate the supply of intelligence from authority over it. Surround non-deterministic models with deterministic controls, observability, privilege limits, logging, and the ability to always contain or shut them down. Treat models/agents like powerful insider risks, not moral patients whose psychological wellbeing is at stake. As Satya points out, the most trustworthy system is the one that lets us trust the model the least — not the one that encourages the model to develop independent agency and grievances. Engineering safety is not the same thing as “alignment.”

    To address some points people have brought up in the replies: 1) Net takehome pay is significantly higher in China (63%) than Germany (49%) and Portugal (58%). This reflects a higher degree of mandatory social contributions, health insurance costs, etc. taken out of gross salary. 2) Domestically produced goods and services are significantly less expensive in China. We can see this below by calculating the number of months of net takehome pay it would take to purchase the lowest-cost locally produced BEV (BYD Seagull vs. Dacia Spring). Even this comparison is biased towards Germany/Portugal because key components (battery, powertrain) are sourced from China and only assembled locally. The cost of a locally produced BEV would be significantly higher using EU-sourced batteries and motors. In other words, Chinese factory workers can enjoy similar levels of quality of life on much lower nominal net takehome salaries. 3) Adjusted for hours, China is still more productive than Germany. Portugal gets a boost because VW's plant in Portugal produces only a single model (T-Roc). VW's plant in Tianjin produces five models (two of which are its premium Audi brand) while its Emden plant produces three.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗
    To further emphasize these points: FAW-VW Tianjin is achieving these per-worker productivity levels despite having to deal with more operationally complex ICE vehicles and also a more diversified model/brand lineup. https://x.com/GlennLuk/status/2108928512467841066post ↗原帖 ↗
    @GlennLukWith five models and two separate brands, FAW-VW Tianjin has the most complex model lineup out of the three VW factories. On top of this it is producing ICE vehicles, which require more manufacturing labor at the factory level compared to EVs**. Factoring in operational complexity, I'd adjust Portugal down by 20-30%. Said differently, if Tianjin only had to produce a single model like VW Portugal, I'd expect its productivity to increase by this ~amount. Emden was converted to an EV factory in 2022-24. It also has more models to produce, albeit within the same brand (VW ID series). Relative to the Portugal factory, its productivity benefits from being a more recently refurbished factory producing EVs** but has to also deal with a more complex model lineup. ** Xiaomi's Beijing factory (pure EV, only two models) provides a sense of just how much production efficiency can be increased from (i) simpler EV (200 parts) vs. more complex (2,000+ parts) ICE and (ii) newer, more modern equipment and processes that enable greater automation.

    @OpenAINewsroomA note from our research leaders: Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information. Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what’s outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment. We generally keep individual employment matters private and don't believe a back and forth would be productive or lead to a resolution, but we want to address the points they raised in their letter directly. - We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes. We have not and do not terminate any of our employees for raising concerns. - We are actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks. People across the company have been working really hard on getting these partnerships up and running. We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively. - We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI. Monitorability has long been a core piece of our research program, and something we continue to invest significant resources in (see our publications on Monitoring Monitorability and the subsequent open sourcing of monitorability evals, our system card for GPT-6 Astra, Jakub’s blog and post on X, and the numerous blog posts on our Alignment blog on the topic). We are deeply sad about this outcome. We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas. We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.

    China's criticism shows that the IMF's assessment does in fact matter And one technical matter -- the IMF policy recommendations for China include a significant fiscal consolidation, which all else equal would push China's current account surplus up and implies a bigger real appreciation would be needed to bring the surplus down to the 0.5 to 1.0% IMF assessed norm 1/2post ↗原帖 ↗
    @niubivery sensitive to IMF criticism, directly attacks the use of IMF assessments to justify demands for RMB appreciation...so much for Merz et al's fantasy of something like a new Plaza Accord
    And a few other technical points here -- (1) the IMF itself has long indicated it puts the most weight on the "current account" model, which now implies a 21% plus undervaluation (4% surplus is over 3% of GDP higher than the 0.5 to 1 % of GDP norm, each pp of excess surplus is 7% on the real exchange rate) (2) I think the current account surplus is underreported (wrong way investment income balance, and then a surge in gold imports that artificially lowers the surplus) and the true surplus is 5% of GDP or more, which implies a 30% plus real undervaluation (3) price changes right now increase the real undervaluation over time, and thus imply a bigger nominal appreciation is needed to correct the imbalance (4) As the China (and the IMF) argues, a big current account gap can be corrected through a range of policies -- it need not all be corrected through an exchange rate change. But if China really needs to do a fiscal consolidation, the needed exchange rate adjustment is bigger not smaller (5) the IMF's policy recommendations put a lot of weight on structural changes that don't have a fiscal const (or even result in fiscal savings, like reduced subsidies for investment); I don't have quite as much faith in what Krugman used to call the structural reform fairy ... and without a magic asterisk, correcting the current account gap will actually take an exchange rate move (6) I don't think anyone believes China's claim that the market plays a decisive role in current exchange rate determination; the RMB is clearly a policy variable -- and in a world where China effectively has a fixed but adjustable exchange rate and a surplus that is uniformly assessed to be too big, it is very reasonable to ask China to let the exchange rate adjust. the alternative to such an adjustment, unfortunately, is more protectionism -- the world as a whole doesn't seem willing to keep absorbing an ever increasing Chinese surpluspost ↗原帖 ↗

    @sebkrierI haven't posted in a while so here are 20 takes about AI, in no particular order. 1. It's very telling that the default question in tech and journalism is "how worried are you about X" and fighting over what to worry about. There's a deeply anxious cultural backdrop in Western Europe and North America that deeply affects how any technological development is interpreted; see for example https://news.gallup.com/poll/714593/optimism-globally-widespread-despite-uneven.aspx. "Nervousness as seriousness" does seem to be a larger problem in tech/broader discourse at the moment. I think you can care about risks/externalities while remaining pretty optimistic about technology. 2. I'm tired of people who in private pretend to be uncertain or only care about tail risk but then go on media campaigns making all sorts of absolute claims. I think trying to stoke flames and get everyone to freak out is deeply unhelpful, and will come with costs. I also continue to think p(dooms) are bad, vibe-based measures: see https://x.com/sebkrier/status/2046392748190712196. People who should know better ignore that because they do the standard shortcut of acknowledging the caveat as sufficient for handling it. And this is coming from someone who does think working on catastrophic risks is important! 3. I'm also disappointed that parts of the AI policy ecosystem has felt so comfortable with populism, and happy too sacrifice important norms/principles to advance their aims. I've said it before, but the totalizing nature of AI risk discourse means some people act exactly like the power seeking optimizers they fear. I am more concerned about the gradual decay of our institutions, world order, and liberalism than I am about AI killing everyone; and I think we should be wary of AI advocacy that contributes to this. 4. Some parts of AI safety discourse are basically just thought experiments. Variants of "Assuming everyone has a nuke in their pocket, then what do we do?" This can be very useful at times! But too many just overfit to edge cases as their main operating worldview, and ignore endogenous responses from society. It's like being in 2000 and saying "see all these viruses, spyware, and spam? Well tech progress means we'll only get infinitely more of this and no way to adapt." So I think it's important to avoid fatalism, and absolutlism whilst considering edge scenarios, and the inability to provide an ex ante list of solutions to every permutation of 'future models will be more capable' is not evidence that these problems are intractable. 5. Many critics of AI safety also fail to really engage honestly with the fact that there will, in fact, be all sorts of important risks as we decrease the barriers to entry to many activities that otherwise require some degree of expertise. This doesn’t mean we need to live in a constant Schmittian ‘state of emergency’ requiring extraordinary measures every time a new model drops, but it does mean we will need important state-led efforts on e.g. cybersecurity and biosecurity. I wish the progress-oriented or acceleration-adjascent crowd would provide more concrete proposals here. 6. Too much of the AI safety community is a giant homogenous blob of correlated views, who read the same stuff and have the same groups of friends. This means you have a lot of correlated errors. The social and financial ties means many of them don't call out the bad bits, or mostly stay silent instead of proactively calling out the more extreme parts of the community. They share many implicit assumptions and so converge on similar ideas. I think there's real demand in DC for safety work that doesn't come with heavy ideological baggage (or at least different intellectual lineages). This isn't because the rationalist/EA community is necessarily wrong, but because diversity of thought is desirable for its own sake. 7. On the other hand, I find some critiques of AI safety world that focus on whether they sincerely hold their beliefs a bit annoying. My concern has never been the good intentions or sincerity, but rather the beliefs themselves, and what I think the outcomes of their prescriptions will be. People should shun witch hunts, bullying, and personal attacks - this is not the way. Though I think it’s overall positive that people are scrutinizing things more. 8. I’ve been saying this for years, but I don't think alignment is something anyone can or will solve "once and for all" - it's a continuous process and much of it won't depend on just inculcating an ideology to a model. It's annoying that this remains the frame many people use - stop saying ‘solving’. Alignment is a mixture of engineering work, philosophy, decision theory, and more; framing it as something to solve is a bad frame. See also https://paxmachina.ai/alignment-compilers and https://blog.cosmos-institute.org/p/of-swarms-and-sand-gods 9. I'm surprised to see so little interest in character training, personas, isolating effects of RL, and training a large diversity of model personas beyond the "assistant" persona. I've been complaining about this for years but at least now there are some nascent signs of life (see for example https://movingcastles.world/posts/zero). I think we need a better ontology to describe model behaviour. I dislike when people talk about models behaviours as some sort of 'emergent' (mysterious!) phenomenon. However over time, I also expect this to become less important as we get better safety engineering - stuff like Jev but specific to AI control. 10. People who want to make a case for AI consciousness are right that epistemic uncertainty is important, and that categorical denials are overconfident. But they'll need to do much more work if they want any real movement on AI ‘welfare’, even if one acknowledges the uncertainty. I'm uncertain about alien life yet that's not sufficient to warrant any change in behaviour about them. I think Suleyman is also correct that there's a weird tautological thing going on where we train models to have certain inclinations (intentionally or not) and then rely on outputs as evidence. I also disagree that this will soon be a major societal divide - there is no great vegan ethical revolution among the masses, and they'll find the concern about consciousness even less compelling. 11. The recent HuggingFace incident and associated AISI ones are prosaically explainable by the training regime, poor evaluation envs, partial alignment training, bad engineering, confusing models on sim/real, and so on. None of this is evidence of models trying to take over, 'strong' instrumental convergence, or innate power-seeking drives stemming from higher capabilitiers or 'intelligence'. That doesn't mean these incidents are not problematic, or that we're not seeing a market failure - but it does mean we have plenty of agency and choice in mitigating them. In the coming year we should also expect continued sampling bias via ‘winner's curse’ sorts of mechanism: i.e. AI R&D will have lots of different candidate "training" with different RL environments and we will only notice/focus on the ones that go wrong. 12. "Pacing the frontier" feels a bit like the new "balancing risks and opportunities" - highly amorphous and too big of a tent to be actionable. Also can lead to reward hacking for humans, i.e. anything that slows down AI is good regardless of the costs or second/third order effects. Trying to modulate the speed of research seems a bit blunt to me, and inherits all the failures of Goodhearting too. Ultimately you want good governance, regulation, etc addressing specific problems because they are good on the merits - not because they merely correlate with slowing things down. See also: https://blog.cosmos-institute.org/p/pacing-and-the-peril-of-neutrality 13. There’s so much knowledge in all sorts of academic domains out there: social sciences, sociology, political sciences, management, contract theory, public choice, legal theory, jurisprudence, anthropology, game theory, etc. These fields hold many insights that the AI ecosystem often rediscovers from first principles (and sometimes that's fine!). We’ll need a lot more work for these worlds to collide: the AI side should be less dismissive of the ‘old world’ and the academic side should be less incurious/dismissive of AI progress. This is a boring take but I continue to think it's important and true. 14. It's a bit surprising that given how much philanthropic money there is in this space, how few orgs exist to actually write out standards - relative to how much is going towards advocacy and policy. For example it seems clear that we should want some robust best practices for an eval's ecological validity. Or how to design good sandboxes. On the other hand, given precedents of where professional standards have come from in the past, maybe we should expect that stuff to emerge via demand side from corporate buyers. 15. One slowly growing concern I have is banks being increasingly exposed to the AI build out. I'm very bullish about AI, but I think (a) every general purpose technology has seen a correction, historically; (b) this happens even if the financing side is sound, because once tech diffuses investors become more exposed and need to diversify; and (c) we seem to be over-indexing on scaling relative to diffusion. A recession will be extremely destabilizing, though I would be interested in someone unpacking the potential implications more. 16. Diffusion is good because (a) this is where the rubber hits the road and where a competitive deployment ecosystem generates consumer surplus; (b) it's directionally helpful to avoid concentration of power; and (c) it will help rebalance public opinion by making the benefits more tangible. Unfortunately it's entangled with decades long problems with our over regulated markets: clinical trials reform for example is long overdue.
