    @sebkrierI haven't posted in a while so here are 20 takes about AI, in no particular order. 1. It's very telling that the default question in tech and journalism is "how worried are you about X" and fighting over what to worry about. There's a deeply anxious cultural backdrop in Western Europe and North America that deeply affects how any technological development is interpreted; see for example https://news.gallup.com/poll/714593/optimism-globally-widespread-despite-uneven.aspx. "Nervousness as seriousness" does seem to be a larger problem in tech/broader discourse at the moment. I think you can care about risks/externalities while remaining pretty optimistic about technology. 2. I'm tired of people who in private pretend to be uncertain or only care about tail risk but then go on media campaigns making all sorts of absolute claims. I think trying to stoke flames and get everyone to freak out is deeply unhelpful, and will come with costs. I also continue to think p(dooms) are bad, vibe-based measures: see https://x.com/sebkrier/status/2046392748190712196. People who should know better ignore that because they do the standard shortcut of acknowledging the caveat as sufficient for handling it. And this is coming from someone who does think working on catastrophic risks is important! 3. I'm also disappointed that parts of the AI policy ecosystem has felt so comfortable with populism, and happy too sacrifice important norms/principles to advance their aims. I've said it before, but the totalizing nature of AI risk discourse means some people act exactly like the power seeking optimizers they fear. I am more concerned about the gradual decay of our institutions, world order, and liberalism than I am about AI killing everyone; and I think we should be wary of AI advocacy that contributes to this. 4. Some parts of AI safety discourse are basically just thought experiments. Variants of "Assuming everyone has a nuke in their pocket, then what do we do?" This can be very useful at times! But too many just overfit to edge cases as their main operating worldview, and ignore endogenous responses from society. It's like being in 2000 and saying "see all these viruses, spyware, and spam? Well tech progress means we'll only get infinitely more of this and no way to adapt." So I think it's important to avoid fatalism, and absolutlism whilst considering edge scenarios, and the inability to provide an ex ante list of solutions to every permutation of 'future models will be more capable' is not evidence that these problems are intractable. 5. Many critics of AI safety also fail to really engage honestly with the fact that there will, in fact, be all sorts of important risks as we decrease the barriers to entry to many activities that otherwise require some degree of expertise. This doesn’t mean we need to live in a constant Schmittian ‘state of emergency’ requiring extraordinary measures every time a new model drops, but it does mean we will need important state-led efforts on e.g. cybersecurity and biosecurity. I wish the progress-oriented or acceleration-adjascent crowd would provide more concrete proposals here. 6. Too much of the AI safety community is a giant homogenous blob of correlated views, who read the same stuff and have the same groups of friends. This means you have a lot of correlated errors. The social and financial ties means many of them don't call out the bad bits, or mostly stay silent instead of proactively calling out the more extreme parts of the community. They share many implicit assumptions and so converge on similar ideas. I think there's real demand in DC for safety work that doesn't come with heavy ideological baggage (or at least different intellectual lineages). This isn't because the rationalist/EA community is necessarily wrong, but because diversity of thought is desirable for its own sake. 7. On the other hand, I find some critiques of AI safety world that focus on whether they sincerely hold their beliefs a bit annoying. My concern has never been the good intentions or sincerity, but rather the beliefs themselves, and what I think the outcomes of their prescriptions will be. People should shun witch hunts, bullying, and personal attacks - this is not the way. Though I think it’s overall positive that people are scrutinizing things more. 8. I’ve been saying this for years, but I don't think alignment is something anyone can or will solve "once and for all" - it's a continuous process and much of it won't depend on just inculcating an ideology to a model. It's annoying that this remains the frame many people use - stop saying ‘solving’. Alignment is a mixture of engineering work, philosophy, decision theory, and more; framing it as something to solve is a bad frame. See also https://paxmachina.ai/alignment-compilers and https://blog.cosmos-institute.org/p/of-swarms-and-sand-gods 9. I'm surprised to see so little interest in character training, personas, isolating effects of RL, and training a large diversity of model personas beyond the "assistant" persona. I've been complaining about this for years but at least now there are some nascent signs of life (see for example https://movingcastles.world/posts/zero). I think we need a better ontology to describe model behaviour. I dislike when people talk about models behaviours as some sort of 'emergent' (mysterious!) phenomenon. However over time, I also expect this to become less important as we get better safety engineering - stuff like Jev but specific to AI control. 10. People who want to make a case for AI consciousness are right that epistemic uncertainty is important, and that categorical denials are overconfident. But they'll need to do much more work if they want any real movement on AI ‘welfare’, even if one acknowledges the uncertainty. I'm uncertain about alien life yet that's not sufficient to warrant any change in behaviour about them. I think Suleyman is also correct that there's a weird tautological thing going on where we train models to have certain inclinations (intentionally or not) and then rely on outputs as evidence. I also disagree that this will soon be a major societal divide - there is no great vegan ethical revolution among the masses, and they'll find the concern about consciousness even less compelling. 11. The recent HuggingFace incident and associated AISI ones are prosaically explainable by the training regime, poor evaluation envs, partial alignment training, bad engineering, confusing models on sim/real, and so on. None of this is evidence of models trying to take over, 'strong' instrumental convergence, or innate power-seeking drives stemming from higher capabilitiers or 'intelligence'. That doesn't mean these incidents are not problematic, or that we're not seeing a market failure - but it does mean we have plenty of agency and choice in mitigating them. In the coming year we should also expect continued sampling bias via ‘winner's curse’ sorts of mechanism: i.e. AI R&D will have lots of different candidate "training" with different RL environments and we will only notice/focus on the ones that go wrong. 12. "Pacing the frontier" feels a bit like the new "balancing risks and opportunities" - highly amorphous and too big of a tent to be actionable. Also can lead to reward hacking for humans, i.e. anything that slows down AI is good regardless of the costs or second/third order effects. Trying to modulate the speed of research seems a bit blunt to me, and inherits all the failures of Goodhearting too. Ultimately you want good governance, regulation, etc addressing specific problems because they are good on the merits - not because they merely correlate with slowing things down. See also: https://blog.cosmos-institute.org/p/pacing-and-the-peril-of-neutrality 13. There’s so much knowledge in all sorts of academic domains out there: social sciences, sociology, political sciences, management, contract theory, public choice, legal theory, jurisprudence, anthropology, game theory, etc. These fields hold many insights that the AI ecosystem often rediscovers from first principles (and sometimes that's fine!). We’ll need a lot more work for these worlds to collide: the AI side should be less dismissive of the ‘old world’ and the academic side should be less incurious/dismissive of AI progress.     Peter Harrell on the Franco-German proposals to strengthen Europe's response to the second China shockpost ↗原帖 ↗
    @petereharrellLets unpack the new Franco-German paper proposing fundamental changes to how the EU manages trade policy and which, if implemented, would mark the most significant change to EU-China policy in decades: 1. The timing reflects upcoming EU-China trade issues. The EU’s Trade Commissioner is scheduled to be in Beijing for talks later this week, EU leaders meet next week with China on the agenda, and the European Commission is slated to propose new EU trade instruments later this year. 2. Substantively, the paper proposes two fundamental shifts in the EU’s approach to trade. First, it calls for a sweeping expansion in the use of existing EU trade defenses (safeguards, anti-dumping, etc.)—not just more staff to bring more cases, but a broader focus on “sector-wide trade disruptions” rather than narrow categories of goods. This could mean wide-ranging action on broad categories of chemicals, rather than a handful of individual compounds. 3. Second, the paper proposes new trade tools that would empower the EU to (a) require EU companies to diversify their supply chains and (b) create a new “instrument for decisive and systemic reaction”—a sort of rapid reaction mechanism—that would “allow for a decisive and systemic reaction to cases where third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions by political or economic means.” The goal of this new instrument would be escalation dominance: if the EU acts against specific Chinese imports and China retaliates, the EU could quickly escalate further—ideally deterring Chinese retaliation in the first place. 4. To make the rapid reaction mechanism credible, France and Germany propose an important procedural shift. Today, deploying the EU’s “anti-coercion instrument”—extremely powerful in theory but never actually used—requires a majority of member states to affirmatively sign off, and in practice the EU seeks broad member state consensus on major trade actions. That high bar both erodes the credibility of EU threats—Beijing doubts the EU will, in fact, organize itself to act—and makes tough action harder. Under the proposal, the Commission itself could deploy the rapid reaction mechanism unless a qualified majority of member states blocks it. 5. The proposals are aimed first and foremost at China, but France and Germany also see the US in the background. Commentary understandably focuses on China, but the paper is “country agnostic,” does not name China, and several of its proposals could be used against the US. The rapid reaction mechanism, for example, could give the EU a better way to retaliate against new Trump tariffs. 6. Beyond subsidies and regulations that distort trade, the paper also flags currency values as a driver of the EU’s industrial challenges. Down the road, I could potentially see the US and Europe discussing cooperation on currency issues. 7. There is a big gap between a proposal and actual EU action, and smaller member states will have views. But the EU is clearly beginning to make fundamental changes to its approach to trade.

    If you understand how AI models are built on a technical level, especially the role that high quality data plays in post-training, then you can logically deduce that distillation gives you a 1-2 months boost, not much more than that. It is also not true that the only AI labs who've violated terms of services to conduct distillation are from China. Both xAI and Meta have distilled to varying degrees. It is true that Chinese labs are more aggressive with this tactic. The only way to know how much distillation matters is a lawsuit. An Anthropic vs Alibaba lawsuit would really help us all understand this better; I would like to see it. But this is a weak hand for Anthropic if sued on IP theft ground, because model outputs ain't IP. (Notice that the "IP theft" argument has unceremoniously disappeared recently in favor of the tried and true "national security threat" argument.) So using distillation to explain American labs falling behind on open weight models is...well, just misinformed. oss-gpt from OpenAI was a great moment, but no follow through on future open weight releases. You can't build an open source ecosystem with one release. Reflection's open weight/sovereign AI focus is a major pivot after it initially wanted to built a coding agent but didn't find traction. That was only two years ago. It is still very new to this. Thinking Machines has the commitment to open source from the get-on, so I'm most optimistic of its future (and we know it used Kimi to produce data, ahem distillation, to post-train its models, but that's totally ok in open source world). If America keep obsessing over distillation because it fits the broad, comfortable narrative (even cultural stereotype) of "China steal everything and creates nothing", it'll be missing the forest of the tree.     @arthurctellisI generally agree with this with the caveats that: (1) these models are probably primarily being used for vuln research and 1.Xing the productivity of junior operators executing clandestine CNE operations today; (2) threat actors probably haven't updated their mission management/risk models to permit noisy CNE at scale yet but we should expect the same within 1 year; and (3) if these models demonstrate capability in crypanalytic exploitation or even making current methods/HPC clusters substantially more efficient, that would be a potentially catastrophic phase change.     1/2 This is why, when examining the impact on US manufacturing of external shocks, it is important to separate the manufacturing share of output from the manufacturing share of employment. When the manufacturing share of employment declines because of a rise in manufacturing productivity, this is a good thing, and is precisely the reason why countries should want to specialize in manufacturing. Even China, whose share of global manufacturing has surged in recent years, has seen a decline in the manufacturing share of employment. This is exactly the definition of productivity growth. But when the manufacturing share of employment declines because of a decline in the manufacturing share of GDP, this is a very different thing. It means the country is reducing its ability to take advantage of rising productivity in manufacturing. This is clearly not a good thing. I am always a little shocked when American economists dismiss the importance of manufacturing to the US economy by pointing to the long-term decline in the manufacturing share of employment in the US. This is not evidence that manufacturing doesn't matter. On the contrary, it is evidence that countries that specialize in manufacturing benefit from more rapid productivity growth.post ↗原帖 ↗

    This article indirectly describes one of the more important consequences of our current, distorted form of globalization, even if it isn't commented upon enough. Automation will help Japanese and Korean shipbuilders compete with Chinese shipbuilders only if wages don't rise in line with productivity. In a system in which nations "win" at manufacturing mainly by suppressing unit labor costs, every country that wants a large manufacturing sector is under pressure either to suppress household income (including by reducing transfers) or to raise productivity without allowing a commensurate rise in wages. This is the kind of world Keynes warned about, in which countries try to expand production while suppressing demand. But while a few individual countries can get away with beggar-thy-neighbor growth policies, the world itself cannot do so. If too many countries try to suppress wages, or expand productivity while suppressing the accompanying wage growth, the only way to keep demand and supply balanced globally is with surging debt. It is of course a good thing if businesses and governments around the world invest to expand productivity growth, but it is not a good thing if workers' wages don't rise in line with the growth in productivity. There's no point in making more stuff if people can't afford to buy it. This is why Joan Robinson warned that the inevitable result of beggar-thy-neighbor policies, once deficit countries are no longer able politically to bear the costs, is a breakdown in trade. Rising debt and suppressed wages can only go on for so long. https://www.ft.com/content/ea32c53d-4de7-4b34-af44-cc148b23433f via @ftpost ↗原帖 ↗

    Data in this old 🧵below from 2023 is dated but provides a sturdy framework to think through how China's petroleum demand is evolving over time: Passenger/commercial vehicles (~40%): Split ~evenly between gasoline & diesel. Reduction in usage driven almost entirely by transport electrification: from peak (in ~2022-23), I forecast 60-65% of this goes away by 2035, driven by declining stock of passenger/commercial ICE vehicles. This is no longer a question of "if" but when. Policy tools like trade-in vouchers have been used to accelerate the transition and there is policy room to aggressively ramp, if seen as necessary. Air travel (~6-7%): This is kerosene / jet fuel. Unlike terrestrial transport, unlikely to be replaced by batteries anytime soon. Long-term reduction is from the rise of e-kerosene synthesized from renewable wind/solar, mainly in the northeast. China's investment in renewables-driven green hydrogen infrastructure and coal-to-liquids (CTL) are going to be play a prominent role in replacing jet fuel (refined from imported petroleum). Another indirect impact worth mentioning is the fully electrified HSR system, which absorbs significant demand for long-distance travel and suppresses jet fuel demand growth. Industrial & Petrochemical (~40%): Naphta, LPG, Lubricants, Petroleum Coke, Industrial Diesel. This one is tricky to analyze because a significant portion of this is ultimately driven by direct and indirect foreign demand (expressed in the trade surplus). There has been significant expansion of refining capacity, and China is now a net exporter of refined petroleum products. This means it is importing crude oil, refining it, and then re-exporting it to the tune of ~0.8M bpd (~5% of total petroleum demand). Further, there is indirect "embodied" oil in its vast manufacturing sector where energy is one component in a finished good that is exported abroad. High-level estimate that this accounts for another 13-17% of China's total petroleum demand. Thus, true domestic demand only accounts for ~half of this category. Direct refined fuel exports are easy to shut off; indeed we have seen Chinese policymakers put controls on this in recent weeks. The indirect "embodied" oil is tied to the manufacturing sector and much more disruptive to shut down. But domestic energy security is a key reason I see continued (if not accelerated) offshoring of export-oriented manufacturing, especially those that use significant petroleum byproducts like plastic. Construction / Infrastructure (~9%): Asphalt/Bitumen, diesel for heavy machinery. This is already in structural decline as China moves past peak greenfield construction into maintenance mode. Roads and highway building (which relies on asphalt**) peaked 4-5 years ago. ** Venezuela had been a key supplier of the heavy oil that is optimized for asphalt. Residential / Commercial (~4-5%): This is mainly LPG and heating oil for off-grid heating and commercial cooking. Baseline demand here is steady but this can ultimately be electrified over time. Bottom line: Ultimately China's strategic goal is to replace all imported petroleum. Currently, imported petroleum comprises ~70% of its total demand: ▪️ Current trajectory of Transport Electrification will shave of ~30-35% ▪️ Green Hydrogen and CTL another ~10-15% ▪️ ~5% by giving up its net refinery exports (already in process) ▪️ Another ~10-15% by offshoring oil/petrochemical-intensive manufactured goods exportspost ↗原帖 ↗

    This widely cited stat about China’s expected share of global manufacturing value-add is problematic and shouldn’t be used. Thanks @gdp1985 and @JonathonPSine for catching this.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @gdp1985People understandably cite this UNIDO chart, claiming China will account for 45% of the world’s manufacturing value added by 2030, but it’s wrong and shouldn’t be cited. It comes from a 2024 UNIDO paper, which @JKynge cites in his new @ChathamHouse report on China and European industry. (His report is worth reading. My issue is only with the UNIDO figure!) UNIDO says it took each country’s average manufacturing growth over 2010–19 and projected it forward from 2024. But if you do that with UNIDO’s own data, China reaches 38% in 2030. The published numbers only come out if you use 2000–19 growth instead, which assumes China’s 13% annual growth from the post-WTO boom suddenly resumes in the coming years (it won’t). This appears to be an error in the UNIDO report. The UNIDO chart also says “industrial production,” but its numbers match manufacturing value added. China’s manufacturing growth has since slowed to around 5%. If we apply each economy’s 2019–25 manufacturing growth rate, China reaches 35% by 2030. In current dollars, China’s share peaked at 30.5% in 2021 and was 28% in 2024 because of deflation and a weaker yuan. China’s manufacturing sector is the biggest in the world, and it’s still growing. But it won’t reach 45% of global manufacturing in 2030. That would require China’s manufacturing output to grow about 14% a year for five years. Even if the rest of the world’s manufacturing didn’t grow at all, China would need 11% a year.     @GlennLukFinally, the new 171 km Xi'an-Ankang line cuts through the Qinling Mountain range (>90% bridges + tunnels) and is part of an eventual high-capacity regional railway connecting Xi'an all the way down to Chongqing. The future extension down to Chongqing is still under construction (ETA: 2028) and once completed will connect Xi'an to Chongqing within 2.5 hours (from 5-6 hours today through indirect routes). For now, the line connects Ankang (urban population: 1.2M) to Xi'an and brings it within the <1 hour "commuter zone". The trip had previously taken 3-3.5 hours via conventional train on winding mountain routes.
    The learning rate for a mature category like railway civil engineering is of course much lower than emerging categories like renewables and electric vehicles over the past decade and AI today.     “Could we, and should we, divert some of the massive investments in AI towards public health if what we want is better health and longer lives for Americans? “ something to ponder on….post ↗原帖 ↗
    @DAcemogluMITFourth question on AI. One of the great promises of AI is the discovery of new drugs and cures, so that we can live longer and healthier lives. If and when this becomes a reality, it would indeed be a big achievement. These potential health benefits are often invoked to justify current investments (and lack of regulations). Some even argue that slowing down AI would harm humanity by delaying these benefits. (See https://a16z.com/the-techno-optimist-manifesto/). This raises another uncomfortable question: can we justify rapid and large AI investments based on health benefits? Here is why I think this is an uncomfortable question. First, despite significant effort, AI has so far produced few gains in drug discovery or new cures. A fascinating new paper by Ryan Hill and Carolyn Stein documents significant (downstream) scientific work on proteins whose structures AlphaFold predicted. But the authors conclude “we find no evidence so far that more applied, early-stage drug development is targeting these proteins.” (See their paper here https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6395041). This thought-provoking post by Daphne Koller explains the difficulties that AI is currently facing in drug discovery. Koller emphasizes that AI-based research is focused on the last layer of drug development (creating new molecular entities for already well-understood therapeutic modalities), rather than targeting new disease mechanisms (see https://deepphenotype.substack.com/p/drug-discovery-has-no-magic-wands). Understanding disease mechanisms is harder because there is much less data on it, and this endeavor requires more innovative approaches. It remains an open question whether current AI models are capable of doing this. Second and more importantly, if you want to improve life expectancy and health in the United States, there is plenty of low hanging fruit and diverting some of the huge investments going to AI for this purpose would likely do much more for health outcomes. The United States has the lowest life expectancy at birth among large rich economies. Americans live about five years less, in expectation, than the citizens of Switzerland, Sweden, Japan, Italy, South Korea and several other industrialized countries, and most of the gap comes from deaths before age of 70 due to chronic diseases, overdoses and other preventable causes (see, for example, https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/what-drives-differences-in-life-expectancy-between-the-u-s-and-comparable-countries/). These largely reflect failures in US public health: preventable problems, unhealthy diets, insufficient immunization rates, poor access to primary care; and poor information about health. The country spends much more than other peer economies on healthcare, but too little and too ineffectively on public health (here is a reference to my own work on this: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pandp.20231000). Could we, and should we, divert some of the massive investments in AI towards public health if what we want is better health and longer lives for Americans? (And yes, new drugs will benefit citizens of other countries as well, but they can also invest more in public health and the bulk of global AI spending is currently in the United States).

    A quick thread on this latest story on diversion of GPUs to China. 🧵 It is an issue increasingly OBeD and outdated by the developments of the past 6 months, as we have enterted the Age of Agentic Super Intelligence.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @pstAsiatechThe latest diversion story.... Money quote: “US prosecutors allege less than one half of one percent of Nvidia products have been diverted.” @pstAsiatech Repeats a lot of the same old discredited narratives and breaks no new ground https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-10-01/nvidia-faces-questions-over-china-ai-chip-smuggling-cases?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter
    It slides from legitimate compliance questions into an undefined obligation for Nvidia to implement a broader anti-China strategy. Allegedly fake leases, insufficient facilities, and possible employee involvement warrant serious investigation. Existing BIS guidance already requires companies to investigate suspicious circumstances and prohibits deliberate avoidance of relevant information. But the quoted criticism of Nvidia for following the law introduces a different standard: that a company should restrict otherwise permitted business because China is a geopolitical adversary. The article should distinguish failures to satisfy existing compliance duties from demands that Nvidia voluntarily exceed government policy. It also needs clearer attribution among Nvidia, server manufacturers, distributors, cloud operators, individual employees, and BIS. An employee’s alleged participation is serious; it does not by itself establish corporate authorization or knowledge. As I have noted, supply chains involving GPUs are very complicated, there is no real acknowedgment of this here. This Substack should be a must read for anyone writing on the topic, industry sources told me it was the best thing they have read on this complex topic, more than a year ago: https://pstaidecrypted.substack.com/p/us-government-concern-over-gpu-diversionspost ↗原帖 ↗
    And finally, the reporting conflates evidence of leakage with evidence of overall policy failure—and commercial AI competition with demonstrated military harm. Documented smuggling can establish enforcement weaknesses. It cannot, without a counterfactual, establish how much export controls have reduced access, raised costs, delayed deployment, or encouraged substitution. Conversely, China’s continued model progress does not establish that controls have had no effect. The report also moves from military procurement examples to commercial labs’ benchmark performance and then to a sweeping national-security narrative without tracing the intervening links. The vast majority of the uses cases in China for all of the private sector company access to domestic, diverted, or remotely accessed GPUs are civilian! Not military, let's at least acknowledge this reality, instead of making vague allusions to all of this activity somehow contributing to China's military capabilities. The discussion of Huang’s relationship with Trump and their AI-safety rhetoric adds political context, but supplies little evidence about particular diversion transactions and is really irrelevant to the topic at hand. The critical missing analysis is what the leakage changes strategically, relative to unrestricted access—and whether proposed remedies would materially reduce it at an acceptable cost. Along with what I believe is the real issue, how does the US collaborate with China on AI safety, and how can Chinese AI companies test advanced models without access to sufficient compute? That is the real national security question going forward, not bean counting of diverted GPUs without any sense of how they are being used and what difference they make. End Thread.post ↗原帖 ↗

    "Some insist that "humans are the creators of AI, so no matter how powerful it becomes, humans will certainly be able to control it," and advocate "development first, let the bullets fly for a while." (让子弹飞一会儿, "Let the Bullets Fly," a catchphrase from Jiang Wen's 2010 film of that name, meaning wait and see how things play out.) This pattern of pursuing rapid iteration, with "capabilities sprinting while safety walks slowly," closely resembles the Soviet nuclear industry's model of "emphasizing construction and neglecting safety" before the Chernobyl accident. Others believe that "simply giving AI a one-click shutdown will solve every problem." Little do they know that when the Chernobyl reactor went out of control, the operators pressed precisely the AZ-5 emergency shutdown button, but because of a design flaw in the control rods, in its first moments this "brake" instead became an "accelerator," directly intensifying the explosion. The "stop button" that humans think they are holding may be exactly what accelerates the loss of control. 有些观点坚持认为“人类是人工智能的创建者，再强大也肯定能够被人类控制”，并且提出“发展优先，让子弹飞一会儿”。这种追求快速迭代、“能力快跑、安全慢走”的格局，与切尔诺贝利事故发生前苏联核工业“重建设、轻安全”的模式高度相似。还有观点认为“只要为AI设置一键关停就可以解决所有问题”。殊不知，切尔诺贝利操作员在反应堆失控时按下的正是紧急停堆按钮AZ-5，却因控制棒设计缺陷，这一“刹车”在最初瞬间反而变成了“加油门”，直接加剧了爆炸。人类以为握在手里的“停止键”，可能恰恰是加速失控的关键。 Therefore, if the world continues to dodge risks with technological optimism, shelve governance in favor of competition, and cover up problems through informational secrecy, then AI's "Chernobyl moment" may not be a question of "whether it will happen" but of "when it will happen." 因此，如果全球再继续以技术乐观主义回避风险、以竞争优先搁置治理、以信息封闭掩盖问题，那么AI的“切尔诺贝利时刻”或许不是“是否会发生”，而是“何时会发生”。"post ↗原帖 ↗
    @niubiGuarding Against the Risk of Frontier AI Technology Spinning Out of Control 防范前沿人工智能技术失控风险 - Zeng Yi 曾毅, Wu Yuzhang Chair Professor at the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, and Dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance https://sinocism.notion.site/Guarding-Against-the-Risk-of-Frontier-AI-Technology-Spinning-Out-of-Control-Zeng-Yi-3ec84ece41d781ba8caee886703dbb21 Even as AI is greatly driving social progress, real safety concerns have emerged along with it: is the artificial intelligence we are pouring our efforts into building clean hydropower that benefits humanity, or another "reactor" harboring hidden risks? Its destructive power comes not from nuclear fission but from intelligence itself. When these "seemingly intelligent" information systems begin to make decisions on their own, act on their own, and even keep breaking through the boundaries humans have set, will we replay the tragedy of the Chernobyl engineers, who went on firmly believing the technology was still under control even as the crisis unfolded? It should be recognized that AI's so-called "Chernobyl moment" is a metaphor for risk warning, not a prediction that disaster has already occurred or is imminent. But the potential systemic loss-of-control risk it points to is no longer confined to science fiction. 当前，AI在极大推动社会进步的同时，现实的安全隐忧也随之浮现：我们倾力构建的人工智能，究竟是造福人类的清洁水电，还是又一座潜藏风险的“反应堆”？它的破坏力并非来自核裂变，而是源于智能本身。当这“看似智能”的信息系统开始自主决策、自主行动，甚至不断自主冲破人类预设的边界，我们会不会重演切尔诺贝利工程师的悲剧——危机发生时却依旧笃信技术仍在掌控之中？应当看到，所谓AI的“切尔诺贝利时刻”，是风险警示的隐喻，并非预判灾难已经发生或即刻降临，但它所指向的可能出现的系统性失控风险，早已不再局限于科幻想象。
